A LOT of people think that doing a hobby for a job will make them happy. It more often than not makes you hate the hobby. SOMETIMES, work and what you love outside work aren't/shouldn't be one in the same. Sometimes work is work. I recommend just talking to people in various industries and asking about their day to day, and doing something you don't hate. You don't need to LOVE your job, but it shouldn't make you miserable. It should provide for the opportunity to do what you want (ie: decent pay, flexible hours, not consistent long shifts etc). Or open your own business, but that has plenty of it's own stress.

I enjoy CNC machining. You get to problem solve for a bit until everything is right, you get to tinker, I'm usually never bothered by anyone. Then you zone out run a few parts and re check that everything is right. Pays pretty good, considering I just kinda wandered into it.
What kind of knowledge do you need to know for CNC? For instance I know CAD. How did you stumble into it?

To just run a CNC you really just need to be able to measure consistently and accurately with a calipers, and be able to figure out how to make minor adjustments on the correct axis as necessary. For instance, if you are cutting out a hole and it's 0.050" too far along the X-axis, adjust it -0.050" in the X-axis offset. Occasionally the program itself will need some minor alterations, such as including cutter-comp.

As to how I stumbled into it, I kept bugging my superiors to learn more positions, even if it was just to be the B-Team Dream-Team for when the regular guy is on vacation. That evolved into me being competent in 8 full time positions, including a leadership position and 3 CNCs, and me being the go-to for pretty much everything. Literally nobody understands the process as a whole better than I do. After a while, one CNC position became open, and I was the logical choice: I've been running that particular one for several months vs every single other applicant being a fresh trainee. Now it is my full time job and I love it, I get to better utilize my skills and problem solve, I make a bit more, there is always more to learn and every day is different.
Do more things. Push yourself outside your normality. Try new shit. You'll never know you like something until you like it.

I started my own business. Didn't have any capital, just a few months of savings to help pay the bills and working my ass off. I had no equipment, office or staff. I started out making $30 dollars a week, but the end of the first month in business, maybe $1000. Not much, but I was excited for the growth and, again, just worked my ass off. I had to make a lot of sacrifices just to make sure the bills were paid. I even had to go to a food bank once just because I didn't want to risk either not paying my bills or not having food for the family.

It's not something I was really passionate about, but I became passionate about it because it is my livelihood. I considered it my last chance at making a decent living for my family. I just don't want to make money, I want to be the best in the industry (which, in turn has rewarded me with making good money). When I meet with potential clients, I tell them even if they don't hire my company what level of service they should expect.

It's a cleaning business, and yeah it's gross sometimes and hard physical work; but I enjoy the customer service side of it. The cleaning side gets me in different environments, is meditative and physical. Sometimes I'm in palatial estates with sprawling acres as the view, other times it's nasty ghetto apartments, seeing various people go about their day outside.

We do a lot of rental properties, and I consider my company part of the sales team. I mean, when people move into an older, but really clean rental, they'll more likely be happy overall with the management. To me, a clean apartment upon move-in is the first sign the management cares about the tenant.

Do you see how ridiculously passionate I am about this? It's fucking cleaning toilets and windows; dirty ovens, refrigerators, making beds with sex toys left everywhere. But I know it's making people happy. Either they don't have to waste their free time cleaning their own house, or a small family can move in to a new place not having to worry about how shitty their new home is.

We're in our 3rd year, I still haven't borrowed any capital, and we're projected to do somewhere around $500k this year. I'd like to make it to $1M in sales annually within 2 years, not for the money, but to know I am making people happy with the work we do.

No one thought I'd make more than maybe $30k just cleaning houses by myself. I was told to "get a real job using my degree." I make more now than I imagined with a "real job", and I'm very happy, despite the stress it brings. There are new challenges every day, and I'm learning a lot about myself in the process.

So, you can do something as shitty as cleaning with little experience and funding and turn into something lucrative. A friend of mine who was skeptical about my business has watched it grow. He finally grew a pair and started his own lawncare/landscaping business - a dream of his for nearly 20 years, but he was too scared.

Another friend of mine just started her own pet-grooming business out of her garage. She was already a groomer, but wanted to do things her own way, and not have to pay a percentage out to a salon. She started out bringing the dogs inside (smaller dogs only) and using her bathtub until she could afford to plumb out an area in the garage for a full-sized wash tub for the dogs.

None of us has had to take out a loan, and we're all doing work we really enjoy. Anyway, if you come up with an idea (services are usually the cheapest type of business to start), feel free to pm me. I've got info on free accounting software, writing operating agreements, and general advice from mistakes I've learned from.
